question.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)=x{z}^{2}-{y}^{3}$ increase most rapidly at the point $(0,1,2)?$
question.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{2}-{y}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{z}^{2}-{y}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{2}-{y}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨{z}^{2},\,-3{y}^{2},\,2xz⟩ \\ ∇g(0,1,2) & =⟨{2}^{2},-3(1)^{2},2(0)(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨4,-3,0⟩.$
